The corresponding pathways are: • Soybean–transesterification–BD, • UCO–transesterification–BD, • Soybean–hydroprocessing–RD, • UCO–hydroprocessing–RD. Here, the first term represents feedstock, followed by conversion technology, and then the final product type. Organic wet waste, including sludge and manure, can be efficiently converted into biocrude through hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) technology (Snowden-Swan et al., 2022a). This HTL biocrude can potentially be used as a liquid fuel blend or further upgraded to RD via hydroprocessing. In this study, a centralized upgrading facility is used for HTL pathways. Key technology components of HTL, such as feedstock preparation, pumping, heating, and the HTL reactor, have reached a TRL level of 6, while current research and development (R&D) focuses on solid separation and aqueous-phase treatment. Pathways considered in this study include: • Sewage sludge–HTL–RD, • Swine manure–HTL–RD, and • Sewage sludge–HTL–biocrude. Both indirect and direct liquefaction are considered for cellulosic woody biomass (represented by a 50% clean pine and 50% forest residue blend in this study). In the indirect routes, biomass is first converted to syngas via gasification (with a TRL around 6–8) (Zhu et al., 2011). After cleanup and reforming, the refined syngas can be converted into (1) RD via the Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process, (2) methanol through methanol synthesis, or (3) DME via methanol dehydration. The corresponding pathways in this study are: • Woody biomass–gasification–methanol, • Woody biomass–gasification–DME, and • Woody biomass–FT–RD. 5 On the other hand, ex-situ catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP) (with a TRL around 6) can convert biomass directly into liquid fuel (Tan et al., 2021). In this process, biomass is decomposed into solid and vapor-phase products in a fast pyrolysis reactor. The vapor phase is then upgraded into liquid CFP bio-oil in an ex-situ catalytic vapor upgrading reactor filled with Pt/TiO catalyst. Like 2 HTL biocrude, CFP bio-oil can potentially be used as a liquid fuel blend or upgraded into RD via hydroprocessing. In this study, CFP bio-oil is co-processed at an existing petroleum refinery. These pathways are, respectively: • Woody biomass–CFP–bio-oil and • Woody biomass–CFP–RD. The ethanol fuel pathways encompass a well-established dry mill technology, with a TRL of 9, to convert corn starch into ethanol, alongside a less mature corn stover to ethanol technology (McAloon et al., 2000; Humbird et al., 2011), respectively: • Corn starch–fermentation–ethanol and • Corn stover–fermentation–ethanol. Currently, most of the ethanol produced in the United States comes from corn via fermentation. Further R&D is needed to enhance the conversion efficiency of lignocellulosic biomass to ethanol, thereby reducing the cost disparity between these two pathways.
